plants.cultivation: cultivated (the only agave legally permitted for tequila)
plants.atAGlance: The only agave legally permitted for tequila; cultivated at scale in Jalisco's valley and highlands.
plants.whereItGrows: Cultivated in the Tequila Valley and the Jalisco highlands (Los Altos), in volcanic and red mineral soils respectively.
plants.harvestProduction: Harvested at maturity (typically 5–7 years); the jimador trims the leaves to the piña, which is then steam-cooked — never sap-collected.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: valley-grown reads savory and vegetal, highland-grown sweeter and more floral; this is place guidance, not a universal flavor.
plants.sustainability: Cultivated, so wild-population pressure is not the concern it is for wild-harvested agaves.

plants.cultivation: cultivated in Oaxaca; wild and cultivated elsewhere
plants.uncertainty: Whether Pacifica/Yaquiana in Sonora is the same plant as espadín or a distinct local variety is debated; the app preserves the regional names without settling the botany.
plants.atAGlance: Mexico's great workhorse agave: espadín in Oaxaca's mezcal, Pacifica/Yaquiana in Sonora's bacanora, chico aguiar in coastal raicilla.
plants.whereItGrows: Valles Centrales of Oaxaca (cultivated), the Sierra de Sonora (wild), and coastal Jalisco (wild and cultivated).
plants.harvestProduction: Cultivated at scale in Oaxaca; wild-harvested in Sonora. Cooked (pit roast or steam), never sap-collected.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: espadín mezcals read roast-forward; bacanora's Pacifica adds Sonoran herbality; flavors differ by place and process, not by the name alone.
plants.sustainability: Wild harvest pressures vary sharply by region: Sonora's bacanora depends on wild yaquiana/Pacifica populations, and mezcal's growth has increased demand on wild-harvested angustifolia relatives elsewhere. Where espadín is cultivated at scale (Oaxaca) the pressure is far lower. Whether Sonora's Pacifica/Yaquiana is the same plant as espadín or a distinct local variety remains debated; this guide preserves the regional names without settling the botany. (Sustainability reporting on wild agave harvest is an active topic in the category press, e.g. Mezcalistas, reviewed 2026-10-21.)

commonNames.name: lechuguilla
commonNames.region: Jalisco highlands (local usage; unrelated to the Sonoran lechuguilla, Agave shrevei)

plants.uncertainty: Local name overlaps with other species in other regions; common names are not globally unique identifiers.
plants.atAGlance: Sierra de Jalisco's signature raicilla agave, wild-harvested; locally also called lechuguilla (unrelated to the Sonoran plant of that name).
plants.whereItGrows: Mountain country of Jalisco's Sierra Occidental, around La Vieja and the Sierra de Talpa.
plants.harvestProduction: Wild-harvested; roasted in above-ground adobe ovens, fermented with wild yeasts, distilled in small batches.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: Sierra raicilla reads herbal and rustic; wild harvest means genuine batch variation.
plants.sustainability: Wild-harvested in Jalisco's Sierra Occidental; raicilla's growing demand puts pressure on wild maximiliana populations, and some producers report replanting programs, though documented evidence is limited. Treated here as a wild-harvest sustainability concern, not a verified producer claim.

plants.cultivation: cultivated; sap collected from the living plant (no cooking)
plants.uncertainty: The 2025 IG declaration for Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas identifies the maguey comiteco as Agave americana L.; some producer/importer and earlier references name Agave atrovirens. The guide records both names rather than silently resolving the difference.
plants.atAGlance: Maguey comiteco, the sap agave of Comitán, Chiapas; the base of comiteco. The 2025 IG declaration identifies it as Agave americana L.; earlier references also name Agave atrovirens.
plants.whereItGrows: Cultivated in the highland plateau of central Chiapas around Comitán de Domínguez.
plants.harvestProduction: Cultivated; the living plant is scraped and its aguamiel collected daily — the piña is never cooked.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: sap-derived comiteco skips roast character entirely; disclosed bottlings may include cane sugars, and composition stays a per-bottle fact.
plants.sustainability: Cultivated; the plant stays alive through sap harvest.

plants.cultivation: cultivated in pulque tradition; sap collected from the living plant
plants.uncertainty: Sources vary on subspecies naming (Manso/Salmiana); the app records the genus-level identity without resolving the subspecies debate.
plants.atAGlance: Maguey pulquero, the sap agave of the pulque heartland; the base of destilado de pulque.
plants.whereItGrows: Cultivated in Tlaxcala and the central-Mexico pulque highlands.
plants.harvestProduction: Cultivated; aguamiel is collected daily from the living plant, fermented into pulque (about 48 hours), then distilled — no cooking.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: sap-derived, so no roast character; sources vary on subspecies naming (Manso/Salmiana), which this guide records without resolving.
plants.sustainability: Cultivated; the plant stays alive through sap harvest.

plants.species: Agave angustifolia and local relatives (identity varies by vinatero)
plants.uncertainty: Tuxca batches may blend several wild agaves; species composition is recorded only when a source documents the actual batch.
plants.atAGlance: The wild agaves of the Jalisco–Colima borderlands — Liñeño, Cimarrón and local relatives — vinateros' raw material for tuxca.
plants.whereItGrows: Southern Jalisco river canyons around Tuxcacuesco and Zapotitlán de Vadillo, reaching toward Colima.
plants.harvestProduction: Wild-harvested; cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation. Ensambles vary by batch.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: batches vary genuinely by vinatero and agave mix; species composition is recorded only when a source documents the actual batch.
plants.sustainability: Wild-harvested; batch composition is evidence-led, never assumed.

plants.cultivation: mostly wild-harvested at high altitude; seed-only reproduction makes cultivation slow, so wild populations are under pressure — some producers now cultivate or reforest (the cited Montelobos entry is 100% cultivated)
plants.uncertainty: Wild vs cultivated tobalá can taste noticeably different; flavor variation between batches is documented and genuine
plants.atAGlance: Tobalá, the small high-altitude 'king of agaves' of Oaxaca's Sierra Norte — mostly wild, some cultivated.
plants.whereItGrows: High mountains of Oaxaca's Sierra Norte (and beyond); 12–15 year maturity at altitude.
plants.harvestProduction: Wild-harvested traditionally; some producers now cultivate or reforest. Pit roast, stone mill, wild fermentation; clay or copper stills.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: typically lighter and more floral than espadín; a cited blind tasting of eight tobalás found no single common thread — wild and cultivated batches taste noticeably different.
plants.sustainability: Seed-only reproduction makes cultivation slow, so wild populations are under pressure from tobalá demand; some producers cultivate or reforest (the cited Montelobos entry is 100% cultivated). As a wild-harvested species with a long maturation cycle, tobala is one of the most-discussed sustainability cases in agave spirits (category reporting reviewed 2026-10-21).

commonNames.name: desert spoon
commonNames.region: Chihuahuan desert (northern México and southwestern USA)

plants.cultivation: wild-harvested, often after roughly 8–12 years (a variable, source-dependent range, not a fixed figure); a single plant may yield roughly one bottle
plants.uncertainty: Not an agave: Dasylirion is a related genus in the Asparagaceae family. This page keeps that distinction explicit.
plants.atAGlance: Desert spoon — sotol's plant. Not an agave: Dasylirion is a related genus in the Asparagaceae family.
plants.whereItGrows: The Chihuahuan desert of northern México (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango), 8–12 years to maturity.
plants.harvestProduction: Wild-harvested; piña pit-roasted in conical ovens (or steam-cooked by larger producers), wild-fermented, distilled in copper or clay. Harvest practice and species determine whether roots are left intact; regrowth is not guaranteed by harvest alone.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: earthy and smoky-herbal; the genus distinction means sotol is never presented as an agave spirit.
plants.sustainability: Wild Dasylirion stands face documented harvest pressure; regrowth after heart harvest depends on species, method and evidence this guide has not verified, so no regeneration claim is made here. Conservation programs address the pressure; cultivation alone would not establish low impact.

plants.cultivation: wild and cultivated; used in Costa raicilla alongside chico aguiar
plants.uncertainty: Common names for coastal Jalisco agaves vary by locality and taberna; the app preserves regional names without resolving species debates.
plants.atAGlance: A coastal-Jalisco raicilla agave, used alongside chico aguiar (angustifolia) in the Costa tradition.
plants.whereItGrows: Coastal mountains and canyons of southwestern Jalisco, around Cabo Corrientes.
plants.harvestProduction: Wild and cultivated; underground pit roast, wild-yeast fermentation, small-batch distillation.
plants.sensoryTendencies: Editorial guidance: contributes to Costa raicilla's profile alongside chico aguiar; common names for coastal Jalisco agaves vary by locality and taberna.
plants.sustainability: Mixed wild/cultivated; regional names are preserved without resolving species debates.
